newsitem.title: CANADA: Peru, Japan leaders in Canada for crisis summit.
newsitem.headline: Peru, Japan leaders in Canada for crisis summit.

text.p: Japanese Prime Minister Ryutaro Hashimoto, fearful of bloodshed in the Lima hostage crisis, said on Friday he would urge Peruvian President Alberto Fujimori to open negotiations with Marxist rebels holding 72 captives.
The leaders arrived separately at Toronto's international airport on Friday for hastily arranged talks on the 45-day hostage standoff at a formal summit scheduled to begin on Saturday morning.
On Friday night Hashimoto paid what Japanese officials described as a "courtesy visit" to Fujimori, which they said lasted one hour. No details were immediately available on their conversation.

The summit was called two days ago as a rift appeared to widen between Lima and Tokyo on talks with Marxist Tupac Amaru Revolutionary Movement (MRTA) rebels who are holding the hostages in the Japanese ambassador's residence in Peru.
Hashimoto told reporters on the plane to Toronto that he would "frankly ask" Fujimori to open negotiations with the MRTA to release the captives, seized on Dec. 17 during a diplomatic reception.
"I do not think starting a dialogue means giving in to terrorism," Hashimoto said.

Peru's talks with the guerrillas have been deadlocked for weeks over Lima's refusal to consider the MRTA demand that the government release their 400 jailed comrades. But Tokyo wants Lima to soften its position and allow the rebels' main demand onto the agenda for negotiations, according to a Japanese government source.
Hashimoto voiced fear that the crisis could end up in bloodshed if the MRTA harmed the hostages, which include about two dozen Japanese businessmen and diplomats.
"If the terrorists harmed the hostages, the situation would completely change," he said.
"President Fujimori's position is very clear," he added.
Fujimori has said he will not storm the residence by force unless a hostage is harmed by the rebels.
The Japanese prime minister said the crisis had reached a "delicate stage," indicating he wants a quick resolution to the crisis.
But the Peruvian leader said he could endure the hostage crisis for months, even raising the specter of the U.S. Embassy crisis in Iran 17 years ago.

"I don't have the faintest idea how long it will be before there is a solution to the crisis. Remember that there was a seizure in Iran that lasted 444 days," Fujimori told Argentina's Clarin newspaper in an interview published after his departure for Canada.
"We are not going to give in to the terrorists' demands. As time goes by, offers made by the government are being progressively reduced," he said.
Among the hostages are Fujimori's brother Pedro, two Cabinet ministers, generals, security chiefs and Bolivia's ambassador to Lima.
Japan's concern deepened this week after provocative action by Peruvian police outside the compound.

Since last Friday, police have stepped up the war of nerves, saying they wanted to wear down the rebels' resistance. They sent convoys rumbling past the residence, blasted martial music and buzzed the residence with helicopters and planes.

The Japanese and Peruvian leaders agreed to meet after Hashimoto urged Fujimori to exercise caution to avoid "accidents or incidents" at the diplomatic compound, strewn with rebel mines and booby traps.

The MRTA's international spokesman on Friday warned that Fujimori was playing a dangerous game by suggesting he could wait weeks or even months rather than accept the rebel demands about freeing the jailed guerrillas.
The spokesman, Isaac Velazco, urged Hashimoto to convince Fujimori to seek a political solution to the crisis.
Fujimori and Hashimoto, who have met twice in the past four months, chose Canada because they wanted to meet on neutral ground at a convenient mid-point.
Fujimori, the son of Japanese immigrants, was accompanied by two cabinet ministers, five congressmen and his son Kenjy.
